newsitem.title: PERU: POLL -Peru's Fujimori rebounds on populist speech.
newsitem.headline: POLL -Peru's Fujimori rebounds on populist speech.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's popularity rebounded following populist measures as 28.5 percent of Peruvians backed him August 1, compared with a record low of 18.8 percent in mid-July, a pollster said Monday.

Fujimori reversed the trend of a political crisis, which had seen him plunge in the polls, by promising in last week's State of the Nation speech to raise wages and reduce a housing tax, Bernardo Verjovsky of Analistas y Consultores said.

But scandals involving the security forces -- including torture and wire-tapping -- and maneuvers to oust the owner of the television station that first broke news of the alleged abuses, still deeply concerned the public, Verjovsky said.

Despite Fujimori's insistence in the July 28 address that the armed forces were subordinate to him, 63 percent of the 400 adults in Lima, who were surveyed, disagreed. A further 69 percent believed media freedoms were not guaranteed in the country.
Another serious problem for Fujimori is his credibility. Sixty-five percent of those polled said they did not "believe in the president's word."

This lack of faith in Fujimori has hurt people's confidence in Peru's future. Forty-three percent said they believed the country would improve, compared with 66 percent at the end of 1996, the last time the pollster posed such a question.
About half of those who approve of Fujimori's government would back Fujimori in a future election.
If the president -- now in his seventh year in office -- decided to run for an unprecedented third term, 14.5 percent said they would vote for him.
Ambiguities in the country's constitution make it unclear if Fujimori can stand for office in the 2000 elections.

Lima Mayor Alberto Andrade is more popular with the electorate thanks to his work remodeling the capital's center and improving its chaotic traffic. In a presidential election, Andrade could count on the vote of 46 percent of those polled, Analistas y Consultores said.
The poll had a 4.5-point margin of error.
